task_row_model.query: How can I remove duplicates from a Python list while preserving the original order, and what are the time and space complexities of the approach?

documents.content: Many Python tutorials present a simple loop-based idiom to remove duplicates while keeping order. The pattern creates an empty set named seen and an empty list named result. For each item in the input sequence, the code checks if the item is not in seen; if not, it adds the item to seen and appends it to result. After iterating, result contains the original items with earlier duplicates removed. This approach uses additional space proportional to the number of unique items and, assuming average-case constant-time membership checks for the set, the loop runs in linear time relative to the input length.

A concise alternative leverages mapping types: list(dict.fromkeys(seq)) returns the unique items of seq in their first-seen order because dicts preserve insertion order (as guaranteed by modern Python implementations). dict.fromkeys constructs a dictionary whose keys are the sequence items; converting the keys back to a list yields the de-duplicated sequence. Constructing the dict and then the list requires space proportional to the number of unique keys and, with average O(1) hashing and insertion, overall linear time in the length of the input sequence.

A blog-style note discusses why sets are so fast: hashed containers typically provide average-case constant-time membership, though worst-case degenerate behavior can occur with pathological inputs. The post digresses into the history of hash tables and contrasts JSON-based de-duplication pipelines in production systems, quoting an unrelated survey about dataset sizes. It speculates that for tiny lists you might not care about asymptotics and repeats definitional boilerplate about what a set and dict are, but does not add new algorithms beyond mentioning set-based and dict-based approaches.

task_row_model.golden_answer: To remove duplicates while preserving order, either iterate over the list, adding unseen items to a set and appending them to a result list, or use list(dict.fromkeys(seq)) since dicts preserve insertion order. Both approaches use O(n) time on average (assuming O(1) membership/insertion) and O(n) additional space proportional to the number of unique items.
